title: Fencing and card-table tactics
core: All three are borrowed from the duel and the game table, and all three name a *move* inside a contest rather than a state of affairs: something one player does to another while the other is still playing. That shared arena is what blurs them — each involves an opponent, an advantage, and a moment. What separates them is direction and stance: one misleads, one gets a move stopped, one gets a move judged. Each also carries a second sense the exam prefers to the obvious one.

words.nuance: The only one that **must be seen to work** — it aims at the opponent's *attention*, a committed-looking movement one way so the real blow lands another. Hence it stays morally clean: fencers, boxers and generals feint and no one calls it dishonest, whereas the other two invite a verdict.

The only **reactive** one — it needs an attempt already in motion (a plot, an escape, a heist) and describes what happens *to* someone else's move; you can't foil an intention. It also casts roles: the foiler is the hero, the foiled faintly absurd. The noun sense abandons combat entirely — a foil doesn't oppose, it *flatters by contrast*, throwing another's qualities into relief.

The only one that is a **verdict rather than a description**: calling something a ploy convicts it of small, cheap self-interest and says the speaker has already seen through it. Scale is built in — one move, not a campaign — and nobody applies it to their own manoeuvre.

exam_note: GRE prefers the off-sense: **foil** almost always means the Watson-to-Holmes contrast, not "thwart" — and it will offer **feint** and **ploy** as interchangeable when only *ploy* carries contempt.
